definition: What a researcher sets out to achieve through their research, for example, to find out why something happens.
A group of learners whose norms and values reject those of the school.
Money paid by governments to people who are ill, unemployed or poor.
The economic system of most countries today; based on private ownership of the means of production.
A closed stratification system in which a group’s status is fixed at birth and cannot be changed.
When a change in one variable has a direct effect on another variable.
When a child’s needs and wishes are the most important considerations.
A couple who live together and have no children.
Disagreement; this term is used to describe a perspective on society which assumes there are basic disagreements between social groups (for example, based on social class or gender differences).
The buying and use of goods and resources.
A lifestyle based on what people buy and consume (rather than, for example, the work they do).
Variations in consumption depending on time, place and group.
When two variables change at the same time, suggesting they are connected.

Where culturally significant practices and artefacts from one part of the world are adopted by people in another part of the world, in a way that uses them as a fashion statement and strips them of their meaning.
Racism based on differences between ways of life, such as religion and customs, rather than supposed biological differences.
When poor people have a different set of values to the majority, which keeps them poor.
When poor families become trapped in poverty for at least three generations because they have no access to the resources or qualifications to lift themselves out of it.
The number of deaths per 1000 people in a population in one year; also called the mortality rate.
Changes in a population, such as the birth rate and death rate.
The way that someone presents themselves online, and the personae they adopt in online communities, such as forums and social media. See also online identities.
The internet and other online sources.
The way in which the wealth and income of a society are divided among its population.
Variety; cultural diversity refers to the wide differences between human cultures.
The formal, legal ending of a marriage.
The way in which tasks in the home (such as cooking, cleaning, childcare and repairs) are divided between men and women.
Families in which both partners do paid work.
A family that fails to carry out the expected functions; for example, where children are neglected.
How well individuals do in the school system, usually measured by exam results.
When different groups (based on class, gender and ethnicity) are treated or educated differently or have different levels of educational achievement.
Moving away from your home country and settling in another.
When everyone has the same chance of succeeding.
A family with parent(s) and children living with or close to other relatives, such as grandparents or aunts and uncles.
The functions of the family; the roles it plays and for whom, according to functionalist theory.
The parts played by different members of a family.
When friendships between people who are not related to each other form a support network similar to a more traditional family.
The ways in which education contributes to society.
Where men and women are treated the same and have equal outcomes in all aspects of society.
A system where one gender has a higher status than the other gender; in a patriarchal society, males benefit from the gender hierarchy.
Differences in experience and outcomes for males and females, based on their gender; for example, in terms of educational achievement.
The roles and expectations associated with being male or female. See also gender.
The way in which societies expect women to be responsible for some tasks (such as cleaning and preparing food) and men for others.
The way that males and females are taught the expectations relating to their gender roles.
The idea that, as a result of globalisation, there is or will be a single culture shared by people all around the world.
Differences in educational provision, outcomes and experience in different countries and regions of the world.
Relating to something that is widely accepted and difficult to escape from.
Written sources from the past used as sources of information by sociologists.
Education of school-aged children in the home, rather than at school.
When the differences between identities of people around the world disappear, so they become similar.
Arriving and settling in a new country.
Socialisation that does not fully instil the shared norms and values of a society; individuals who are inadequately socialised are more likely to become deviant.
Ways in which the interviewer asks questions or interprets answers that have an effect on the findings
Ways in which an interviewer may influence participants’ responses, for example through their characteristics, appearance or verbal cues, such as facial expressions and tone of voice.
The typical way of life of an individual, group or culture.
One parent and their dependent children living together. See also one-parent family and single-parent family.
A marriage where the couple decide to get married, with or without the consent of their families.
Approaches that take a large-scale view of whole societies.
The formal joining of a man and a woman in a relationship with rights and responsibilities; some countries now allow same-sex marriage (involving two men or two women).
When a label becomes the single most important thing about a person in the eyes of others, and is then internalised by the labelled person.
The content of newspapers, magazines, film, television and radio programmes and other forms of media.
Approaches that take a small-scale view of social interaction between individuals and groups in society.
Hatred of women, primarily by men.
The severe exploitation of vulnerable people for personal or commercial gain.
A society in which many different cultures or sub-cultures exist alongside each other.
Closed questions with a number of answers from which the respondent has to choose the correct option.
Statistical data produced by other organisations, such as charities and think-tanks.
Schools which accept all learners, regardless of ability.
The subjects that are taught and the content to be covered.
Statistical data produced by government and official agencies.
One parent and their dependent children living together. See also lone parent family and single-parent family.
When only one person lives in a residence. See also single person household.
The way that someone presents themselves online, and the personae they adopt in online communities, such as forums and social media. See also digital self.
Distance education delivered electronically, via the internet, using digital technology.
Groups of people who connect with each other online, through social media or other websites. They share distinct norms and values, often related to a particular interest or issue.
Exclude someone from a community or group.
Links between different variables, for example, gender, ethnicity or age.
People of the same status (for example, people the same age).
Documents such as letters and diaries produced by individuals for their own purposes.
Ways of viewing society and social life.
In a postmodern society, people can choose from a range of options and select what suits them best.
Middle-aged adults who care for their ageing parents, as well as for their children. See also sandwich generation.
Education which breaks away from traditional lessons and curriculum and focuses on experience.
When those who earn more pay a higher rate of tax on some of their earnings than those who earn less.
A group of learners whose norms and values agree with those of the school.
A group of people who protest in order to bring about a change in society.
The transfer of some of the income and wealth from richer individuals to those who are poorer, through systems such as taxation and welfare payments.
Feeling disadvantaged in comparison to others in your society.
The idea that all cultures vary and change; culture is not fixed, but relative to time and place.
A sub-culture based on religious faith and practices which are distinct from those of the wider culture.
People who are employed when an economy is booming or when they are needed, but who find themselves out of work when they are not required.
The proportion of people in the original sample who actually take part in the research, for example, by completing and returning the questionnaire.
When someone acts as an example, so their behaviour is copied by others.
The group of people on whom research is carried out, used to represent the target population.
The different ways in which samples can be chosen.
Middle-aged adults who care for their ageing parents, as well as for their children. See also pivot generation.
Closed questions where the possible answers cover a range of statements or opinions.
The way in which scientists work, by observing, formulating and testing hypotheses, analysing the results and drawing conclusions.
When schools choose their learners, usually based on their ability.
Research that asks people what crimes or deviant acts they have committed.
When children are taught a particular subject with other children of a similar ability.
One parent and their dependent children living together. See also lone parent family and one-parent family.
The sense of belonging and amount of connectedness between groups in society.
Acting in accordance with norms and social expectations in order to fit in with others.
The assignment of different roles and statuses to groups and individuals within a society.
When society does not provide a group with the rights and benefits available to others in the same society.
Laws, values, customs and other social rules over which individuals have no control.
Things that affect lifestyle and life chances, such as wealth, religion and occupation.
The process of learning the norms and values of a culture.
The differences between groups in a stratification system; for example, in income or wealth.
Internet-based applications for sharing content and communicating online, such as Instagram and Weibo.
When all learners take the same assessments, which are marked in the same way.
A position that someone has in a society; status can be ascribed (fixed by others) or achieved.
Applying and acting upon an oversimplified set of ideas about a particular type of person or social group.
A group of people within a larger culture which has its own distinctive norms and values.
Large-scale pieces of research which tend to generate quantitative data through methods such as questionnaires or structured interviews.
When there is a regular pattern in selecting from the sampling frame, for example, every tenth name on a list.
The whole group that the research relates to and to whom the findings of the research will be applied.
Changes over time in a particular direction.
When the government pays everyone a fixed amount of money as a regular income.
Schooling provided for all children, regardless of their background.
Informal learning without lessons or a curriculum, in which the learner chooses what and how to learn.
An online group of individuals who share interests, personal opinions or backgrounds.
A sub-culture of adolescents or young adults who are usually distinguishable by their style, dress and / or musical preferences.
